summary: The proposal's core bypass posture is sound — front-matter `Bypass-surface non-empty: false` holds, the implicit-exclusion set is honestly enumerated, and D-022/D-031/D-036 characterisations are accurate. Three issues require inline fixes before merge: (1) the §3.4 implementation sketch creates a hard cross-rule dependency on `scp_r_002_is_waiver_payload` and `scp_r_002_has_nonempty_string` that silently breaks SCP-R-004 if SCP-R-002 is ever refactored, (2) §5 understates the trivial-URL bypass surface (a malicious actor can satisfy the rule with `reason: 'https://x'`), and (3) the meta-waiver description in §5 is operationally misleading — a SCP-R-004 waiver whose own `reason` lacks a URL is itself a raw finding, requiring either a URL in the meta-waiver's reason or rule-config disable.

findings.description: The implementation sketch for `scp_r_004_raw_findings` directly reuses `scp_r_002_is_waiver_payload` and `scp_r_002_has_nonempty_string`, both defined in `policies/SCP-R-002.rego`'s `package main`. This cross-rule dependency is undocumented in §5 and is a silent-bypass risk: if SCP-R-002 is refactored (e.g. the guard renamed as part of TF-008's path-scoping work), SCP-R-004's `raw_findings` rule becomes undefined at compile time and produces zero raw findings — effectively making SCP-R-004 a silent no-op without any error surface at the Rego evaluation layer. The proposal's §5 correctly states 'No new `.scp/rule-config.yaml` key' but does not enumerate cross-rule Rego coupling as a bypass-adjacent risk.
findings.recommendation: Inline fix in §3.4: (a) define SCP-R-004's own `scp_r_004_is_waiver_payload` predicate (identical to SCP-R-002's guard: `is_array(input)`) rather than calling `scp_r_002_is_waiver_payload`; (b) define SCP-R-004's own `scp_r_004_has_nonempty_string` or reference the common `scp_common.rego` helper if one is lifted there. Add a note in §11 References under 'Related rules': 'Phase-2 implementation MUST NOT call `scp_r_002_*` predicates directly; if the helpers are needed in multiple rules, they are promoted to `policies/scp_common.rego` as part of the Phase-2 PR.' This keeps the rule self-contained and prevents a TF-008 refactor from silently disabling SCP-R-004.

findings.description: §5 states 'Bypass surface: None' but does not enumerate the trivial-URL bypass: a malicious actor can satisfy SCP-R-004 with `reason: 'https://x'` or any syntactically valid URL that points at an unrelated or nonexistent resource. §4 FP-3 acknowledges this as 'Adversarial-only' and marks it out-of-scope at v1.1.0, but §5 should explicitly name it as a known residual bypass within the 'implicit-exclusion set' section rather than leaving it to §4 alone. The current §5 text creates a false impression that the rule has zero bypass surface, when in fact it has a known minimal-effort bypass that relies on operator review to catch. Reviewers approving on the basis of '§5 = None' may not notice that FP-3 documents the actual bypass.
findings.recommendation: Inline fix in §5: add a fifth implicit-exclusion case (or a 'Residual known bypass' subsection): '5. **Reason contains a syntactically valid URL that does not point at a decision artifact** (`regex.match(...)` returns true on any `https?://` string including `https://x`). This is the rule's known honest-posture minimum: SCP-R-004 enforces "a URL exists", not "the URL resolves to a decision artifact". Adversarial adopters can construct a meaningless URL; this is accepted as a v1.1.0 limitation (see §4 FP-3). A future SCP-R-005 proposing domain-allowlist narrowing would move this from residual to closed.' This makes the bypass explicit in §5 without changing the acceptance scope.

findings.description: §5's third bullet states 'Such a waiver would have `reason` text without a URL — meta-recursive, but legitimate as a one-off; the operator approves it through the standard waiver path.' This is operationally misleading. A waiver against SCP-R-004 whose own `reason` field lacks a URL is itself a raw finding for SCP-R-004 (because SCP-R-004 fires on every waiver entry in the waivers payload that has a non-empty reason without a URL). The operator cannot simply add a URL-less meta-waiver and have it suppress SCP-R-004 on itself — the meta-waiver would itself trigger the rule. The operator's actual options are: (a) include a URL in the meta-waiver's `reason` (at which point it is self-satisfying); (b) use rule-config disable instead of a waiver. The current text implies option (b) is the only bypass path but suggests that a URL-less meta-waiver 'works' through the standard waiver path, which it does not without a URL.
findings.recommendation: Inline fix in §5 third bullet: replace 'Such a waiver would have `reason` text without a URL — meta-recursive, but legitimate as a one-off' with: 'Such a waiver MUST itself contain a URL in its `reason` field (e.g. `reason: "waiving SCP-R-004 for legacy waivers per https://github.com/.../issues/NNN"`) — otherwise the meta-waiver is itself a raw finding for SCP-R-004. An operator who cannot supply a URL in the meta-waiver reason should instead use `.scp/rule-config.yaml disable: true` for the transition period.' Also update §8.1 `test_waiver_suppresses_via_scp_r_004_waiver` test description to clarify that the test waiver must have a URL in its reason (since `scp_active_waiver_for` reads from `data.waivers`, not `input`, the test data must reflect this).

findings.description: Dispatch-note criterion (xiv) requires 'PR description includes one-paragraph Bypass surface enumeration' for this non-bypass proposal. `README.md` §2 (lines 57-67) states the explicit 'Bypass surface enumeration' paragraph in the PR description is REQUIRED only for bypass-introducing proposals (`Bypass-surface non-empty: true`); for non-bypass proposals ('Window (non-bypass proposals)' subsection) no such paragraph is required — the window is waivable and no special PR-description content is mandated. Criterion (xiv) over-promises: it would require future non-bypass proposal PRs to include an enumeration paragraph that README.md explicitly reserves for the bypass-introducing variant. If (xiv) is operationally enforced, it creates a process inconsistency where non-bypass proposals face a documentation burden not required by the governing process document.
findings.recommendation: Inline fix in DISPATCH-NOTE.md criterion (xiv): change to 'PR description includes a one-sentence Bypass surface statement (e.g. "None — §5 confirms `Bypass-surface non-empty: false`"). Full enumeration paragraph is REQUIRED only for bypass-introducing proposals per `README.md` §2.' This aligns the slice acceptance criterion with README.md's process definition and avoids inflating the non-bypass review burden.

findings.description: The `warn` rule sketch in §3.4 fires only when `count(scp_r_004_raw_findings) > 0` AND a matching unexpired waiver exists OR rule-config is disabled. This mirrors the existing SCP-R-001/002/003 warn pattern and is correct — the `warn` rule emits suppression-observability records, not per-finding notifications. However the sketch contains `record := { "kind": "waiver", "rule_id": scp_r_004_rule_id, ... }` with a literal `...` placeholder, making it non-evaluable as written. Phase-2 implementation will fill this in, but leaving `...` in the merged proposal sketch (which becomes the canonical specification) could cause a Phase-2 implementer to miss required fields (compare the fully-specified warn record shapes in SCP-R-001/002/003 which include `waiver_id`, `finding_id`, `expires_at`, `file`, `msg`).
findings.recommendation: Inline fix in §3.4: expand the warn record shape to match the SCP-R-001/002/003 pattern, replacing `...` with `"waiver_id": object.get(w, "waiver_id", ""), "finding_id": object.get(w, "finding_id", ""), "expires_at": object.get(w, "expires_at", ""), "file": "output/findings/waivers.json", "msg": sprintf(...)`. This keeps the sketch as an accurate implementation guide and prevents field-omission drift in Phase 2.

findings.description: §3.1 states the URL pattern is `https://[^\s]+` (HTTPS only) while §3.4 correctly shows `https?://[^\s]+` (HTTP or HTTPS). The mismatch between the plain-English spec section (§3.1) and the Rego sketch (§3.4) means a reader of §3.1 alone would conclude HTTP URLs are not accepted, contradicting the §10 deferrable resolution ('accept both at v1.1.0'). The 'Open questions' resolution for the HTTP question is buried in §10; the contradiction in §3.1 creates a specification inconsistency.
findings.recommendation: Inline fix in §3.1: change `https://[^\s]+` to `https?://[^\s]+` in the match-condition bullet. Add the parenthetical '(HTTP or HTTPS; see §10 deferrable resolution on HTTP acceptance)'.
